facts.raw_span: A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia
he had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering”
two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015
biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
he reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges
abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV
after angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved
follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma
MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis

concepts.why: The patient has a history of two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, which were biopsied and shown to be adenomas without malignancy, and recent imaging confirmed active bleeding from one of these lesions.
The patient presented with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia, and imaging studies revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding and active bleeding from a hypervascular liver lesion.
The patient was admitted with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia, and laboratory studies showed a low hemoglobin level.
The patient has a history of two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, and recent imaging confirmed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma.
The patient's hypervascular liver lesions showed central necrosis on MRI, raising suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, although the lesions did not have typical features of HCC.
The patient presented with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia, and imaging studies revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding, indicating gastrointestinal bleeding.
The patient was on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal 'pre-shimmering', indicating a coagulopathy.
The patient presented with acute-onset abdominal pain, which was severe enough to require hospital admission.

rationales.F01: Acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia suggest a possible hepatic hemorrhage or gastrointestinal bleeding.
rationales.F03: Hypervascular liver lesions are commonly associated with hepatic adenoma and hypervascular liver lesions.
rationales.F04: Biopsy-proven adenoma without malignancy strongly supports the diagnosis of hepatic adenoma.
rationales.F08: Subcapsular hepatic bleeding is a characteristic feature of hepatic hemorrhage.
rationales.F09: Active bleeding from a hypervascular lesion in segment IV confirms the diagnosis of hepatic hemorrhage.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's history of two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015, and the confirmation of active bleeding from one of these lesions, supports Hypervascular Liver Lesion as the champion. Hepatic Adenoma is a close runner-up due to the histologically proven adenoma without malignancy, but the presence of active bleeding and the lack of typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma on follow-up CT scans makes Hypervascular Liver Lesion a more comprehensive explanation.
